https://enrsi.stvr.sk/articles/news/4545.text: More than half a million visitors came to Bratislava during the first five months of 2026, with overnight stays increasing by 17.6 percent year-on-year. Visitor numbers were also 2.4 percent higher than in the record-breaking year of 2019, putting the capital on track for its most successful tourism year yet, according to the Bratislava Tourist Board (BTB). The BTB attributed the growth to improved air connectivity. "Routes with high visitor potential, such as Berlin, Rome, London and Barcelona, are particularly important for us," said BTB Board Chair Nina Erneker. The sharpest increase came from Italy, where visitor numbers more than doubled year-on-year (+104 percent) following the launch of new air routes and were 73.3 percent higher than in 2019. The number of visitors from Norway also rose significantly after a direct flight from Oslo was introduced, increasing by 52.5 percent year-on-year and by 176.7 percent compared with 2019. Growth was also recorded in traditional source markets. The number of Polish visitors increased by 5.6 percent year-on-year and by 37.8 percent compared with 2019 following the launch of a new route from Warsaw. Visitors from Germany rose by 3.9 percent year-on-year and by 16.3 percent compared with 2019, supported by flights from Dortmund and Berlin. Source: TASR

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Police will not allege that either of the teenage boys was the gunman in the shooting death of a university student in Sydney this month. Photograph: Max Aldred/AAP View image in fullscreen Police will not allege that either of the teenage boys was the gunman in the shooting death of a university student in Sydney this month. Photograph: Max Aldred/AAP New South Wales Teenage boys charged with murder after alleged mistaken identity shooting of Sydney student Boys aged 14 and 16 charged after Marco Tapia, 23, was killed inside his family’s home in Glen Alpine Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Nick Visser Wed 16 Sep 2026 20.42 EDT First published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 18.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two teenage boys have been charged with murder after the shooting death of a university student in Sydney this month, which police say was a case of mistaken identity. Marco Tapia, 23, was shot inside his family’s home in Glen Alpine early on 1 September. Officers were called to the house just before 4am that day by reports of a home invasion. They found Tapia with a gunshot wound; he died at the scene. Detectives conducted an extensive investigation, determining that the wrong house had been targeted. Two boys, aged 14 and 16, were arrested on Wednesday and charged with murder. They are not alleged to have shot the weapon. Both face charges of participating in a criminal group contributing to criminal activity, possession of an unauthorised firearm and driving conveyances taken without the owners’ consent. View image in fullscreen Police will allege there were three main offenders that entered the house during the home invasion. Photograph: Max Aldred/AAP The 14-year-old was also charged with damaging property with fire or an explosion. Police will allege in court that the pair staged vehicles and provided a weapon for the gunman. They have been refused bail and will appear in children’s court on Thursday. Hallmarks of organised crime: police Detective superintendent Joe Doueihi, commander of the New South Wales police homicide squad, said police believe there were three main offenders that entered the house during the home invasion and committed the alleged shooting, saying the incident has “all the hallmarks of an organised crime murder”. He went on to say the boys’ alleged involvement was shocking and the charges reflect their alleged knowledge of the episode. “Even those these boys were not present and not part of the actual murder, we will allege that by the nature of their activities they form part of the joint criminal enterprise, therefore they are liable for the offence of murder,” he said during a media conference. “We obviously allege by the fact that we charged them with murder, that they were aware of what their actions were and that they were significantly involved in this crime.” He said police would allege the boys “prepared cars, they dropped cars off. They picked up the offenders. They dropped off the offenders, they supplied a firearm, they burnt the car.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Doueihi said the charges came amid “clumsy” behaviour that left a “trail of evidence”. One of the boys allegedly lit the car used in the attack on fire, but burnt himself in the process and wound up in hospital. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “Both young, both vulnerable, young naive children,” he said. “Both still at school. I’m at a loss as to why these people were enticed into this type of crime.” “They are easily lured by the thrill and the financial incentive. That’s a short-term gain for significantly long term consequences.” ‘Hate came to our house’ Tapia’s parents spoke to Channel Nine’s A Current Affair this week, saying: “Hate came to our house.” Both were home at the time, as was their daughter. “I remember him taking the last breath,” his mother, Claudia, told the program. His father, Sergio, said: “He was a beautiful young man. It’s already impacted a lot of hearts to see such a beautiful person, such a caring, loving man pass in this awful manner. “It was wasteful, it was useless, it was ridiculously stupid to take such a beautiful person away from this earth.” The NSW police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, has vowed to target those behind a spate of Sydney shootings. Another man was killed on 2 September. “One innocent victim is unacceptable to me,” he told reporters after Tapia’s death. “We won’t rest until we stop this violence … anything we can do to stop it, we will do.” Explore more on these topics New South Wales Sydney news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.hindustantimes.com/world-new.text: The United States has resumed processing immigrant visa applications in Hungary and Poland while a broader pause on immigrant visa appointments remains in place elsewhere, Reuters reported, citing four people familiar with the matter.According to the Reuters, the White House directed US missions in the two European countries to prioritize immigrant visa processing last week. The reason for the decision was not immediately clear.The development comes after the Trump administration introduced sweeping measures aimed at restricting both illegal and legal migration.Why Hungary and Poland were singled outThe decision to resume processing in Hungary and Poland comes against the backdrop of President Donald Trump's close political ties with leaders and nationalist movements in both countries. Trump has publicly supported Hungary's former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who lost an April election, as well as Poland's nationalist President Karol Nawrocki, whose election has brought him into conflict with centrist Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government, Reuters reported.ALSO READ: US freezes Cognizant Green Card filings as Trump administration puts employment-based immigration under fresh scrutinyThe White House referred questions about the decision to the State Department. A State Department spokesperson did not explain why immigrant visa processing had resumed in the two countries.Officials in Hungary and Poland also did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment.Wider immigrant visa pause remainsThe US State Department had temporarily suspended immigrant visa processing in 75 countries in January, saying applicants in those countries were considered at high risk of becoming a “public charge.”A federal judge later struck down that policy on August 21, ruling that it was unlawful. Following the ruling, however, the State Department instructed US missions around the world to cancel or reschedule immigrant visa appointments while staff underwent new training.The department said the training was designed to help consular officers assess whether applicants could support themselves in the United States without relying on public benefits.The State Department told a court that interviews would be suspended only through August 31. But Reuters reported that the wider disruption could continue for months because each US mission must complete the training and have a consular officer certified on the new procedures.ALSO READ: H-1B crackdown: US to tighten scrutiny as workers hired after programmers found doing higher-paid jobsImpact on applicants worldwideThe uncertainty extends well beyond Europe. Reuters reported that people in countries including India, Peru and the United Kingdom have posted online about immigrant visa appointments being cancelled through September.Immigrant visas are issued to people seeking to move permanently to the US, including relatives of American citizens and lawful permanent residents. The United States issued about 600,000 immigrant visas in 2024, according to Reuters.The latest development means Hungary and Poland have effectively moved ahead of applicants in many other countries as the State Department works through the consequences of the court ruling and implements its new vetting procedures.For applicants still facing cancelled or delayed appointments, the timeline remains uncertain. As per the report, the new training program could keep the broader pause in place for months, even though the administration's original court filing indicated a shorter suspension.

https://www.trend.az/world/europe/422519.text: Home World Europe EU Commission approves €125.8M for three renewable energy projects Europe News 17 September 2026 15:48 (UTC +04:00) Photo: European Commission Laman Zeynalova Read more BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 17. The European Commission has approved grants totaling €125.81 million to finance works on three cross-border renewable energy projects, according to a statement from the European Commission. Two of the projects involve cross-border district heating systems between Germany and Poland, while the third supports the development of a cross-border onshore wind farm near the Latvia-Lithuania border. The projects are being funded through the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) Energy under the EU budget. They are expected to support investment in energy infrastructure, advance the EU’s decarbonization goals and strengthen energy integration among member states. The largest grant, €70 million, was awarded to the UNITED HEAT project, which aims to develop climate-neutral district heating systems in the twin cities of Görlitz, Germany, and Zgorzelec, Poland. The funding will cover the final works phase, including construction of a cross-border pipeline to enable physical heat exchange and system balancing between the two district heating networks. The pipeline will also integrate heat sources developed under earlier phases of the project. A further €11.41 million will go to the TWIN HEAT project, which seeks to decarbonize district heating in Słubice, Poland, while supporting the transition toward lower-carbon heating in Frankfurt (Oder), Germany. The project will replace existing coal-fired heating units in Słubice with two biomass boilers, each with a thermal capacity of 6 MW, using sustainably sourced wood chips. The third project, UELJO, will receive €44.40 million for its first development phase. The project envisages a cross-border onshore wind farm near the Latvia-Lithuania border comprising around 30 wind turbines and generating up to 680 GWh of renewable electricity annually. The grant will support works in Latvia, including construction of balance-of-plant infrastructure, grid connection works and installation of wind turbines. The European Commission granted the UELJO project Cross-Border Renewable Energy (CB RES) status in 2025, while UNITED HEAT received the status in 2022. The TWIN HEAT project is part of the EU’s efforts to promote coordinated renewable energy development across member states. The EU has progressively strengthened its renewable energy targets as part of its broader climate and energy policy. Building on the 20% renewable energy target set for 2020, the revised Renewable Energy Directive adopted in 2018 established a binding EU-wide target of at least 32% by 2030, with the possibility of a subsequent upward revision. Following the launch of the European Green Deal in 2019, the European Commission proposed in July 2021 to raise the 2030 target to at least 40% of the EU’s overall energy mix. The target was subsequently increased further under the REPowerEU plan, presented by the European Commission in May 2022 in response to the energy crisis following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The plan aimed to accelerate the clean energy transition, reduce the EU’s dependence on Russian fossil fuels and diversify energy supplies. As part of the initiative, the Commission proposed raising the renewable energy target to 45% by 2030. The revised Renewable Energy Directive (EU) 2023/2413, which entered into force in November 2023, ultimately set a binding minimum target of 42.5% for renewables in the EU’s energy mix by 2030, while aiming for a 45% share. The EU has also introduced measures to accelerate renewable energy deployment, including faster permitting procedures for renewable projects and measures to facilitate power purchase agreements. https://www.politico.eu/sponsored-conten.text: European organizations have to reckon with how to keep up with the modern world without sacrificing sovereignty. Geopolitical instability, tightening regulatory expectations and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) mean that, for many organizations, sovereignty now sits alongside resilience and business continuity in board-level risk discussions. The question they can no longer defer is how to harness the opportunities of the modern cloud without surrendering control over their own data. Answering it requires honesty about what sovereignty means, and about where it can actually be found. A definition Europe can trust The European Commission’s forthcoming Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) is the right vehicle for that honesty: giving Europe a shared, enforceable definition of what “sovereign” actually means. Without such a definition, the market is filled with commercial offerings that claim the sovereignty label without delivering the substance, a practice described as “sovereignty washing.” This gap has led some organizations to treat open source as the answer. But open source software is a licensing model, not an operating model, and it doesn’t settle questions about infrastructure or jurisdiction or even reliability and access. It’s not a route out of dependency, it’s a different dependency on project sponsors and code maintainers. A definition gives policymakers a way to properly assess claims of sovereignty against a consistent standard rather than taking marketing at face value. Advertisement Europe should not wait for CADA to take effect before acting, though. European cloud service providers (CSPs) have been partnering with established technology providers to deliver real sovereign capability, without rebuilding the entire technology stack from scratch. The best time to plant the sovereign tree was 10 years ago If Europe wants to grow its industrial base, it has to support the ecosystem as it is now, not as it may in 10 years’ time. CADA’s own roadmap assumes roughly five to seven years to triple the EU’s data-center capacity. Providers who have already built capacity by blending EU capabilities with proven non-EU technologies would have to spend the intervening years relinquishing their growth. It is scale, not a shortage of skills or innovation, that is the biggest practical obstacle facing a stronger European cloud market. This is precisely why partnership with proven technology sources deserves a central place in the sovereignty debate rather than being treated as a second-best option. Partnership shortens that timeline considerably, letting European CSPs deliver sovereign, scaled services now instead of waiting for domestic capacity to catch up organically. In Italy, IPZS, owned by the Italian Ministry of Economy and Finance, is using this model to build a modern Digital Application Platform for the Italian EUDI wallet, a foundational EU digital identity initiative. It provides a live example of that model working in Europe today, at the scale and speed the policy window demands. It is through scale that the local industrial base can deliver sovereign capabilities, compete, capture market share, and invest in developing and integrating home-grown technologies. Hoping for the alternative to happen, that is for a European technological stack to fully emerge and be adopted, is the equivalent of putting the cart before the horse. The rules need to allow for a model that’s already working Advertisement Providers, such as evoila, are now operating well beyond Europe’s borders, alongside Uniserver. This shows the model working at a broader scale, combining local operational and jurisdictional control with proven technology. Sovereignty spans jurisdictional, technological, operational and supply-chain dimensions, and a partnership model can address all four while drawing on technology already proven at scale, rather than asking every layer to be rebuilt from first principles by a single European provider. Alongside its cloud platform, developed in-house and operated from data centers in Europe under EU jurisdiction, IONOS also offers customers a dedicated VMware-based private cloud. It is also operated within the EU and designed to provide European data sovereignty and operational control. Broadcom’s role in that model is deliberately narrow. It supplies the VMware cloud software layer to the CSP, while the CSP itself runs the infrastructure and holds the customer relationship, so that no European customer data passes through Broadcom or is subject to its access. Trust, in this model, follows the architecture rather than the brand. If CADA’s tiers implicitly assume that sovereignty can only be delivered by a fully European-built stack, CADA would shut out precisely the route that is already allowing Europe to scale fastest: partnership between local operators and proven technology providers. The path forward Europe does not have to choose between moving quickly and building sovereignty. The two are compatible, provided the legislation is calibrated to recognize it. As the European Parliament and European Council work on CADA, the priority should be for it to recognize and reward the partnership models already delivering sovereign capability across Europe today.
